chapter_title: Measurement and Interpretation of Consolidation Properties of Soil

sections.title: Consolidation Test Methods
sections.summary: Two main laboratory consolidation test types: (1) incremental load (IL) — load applied in increments with LIR ≈ 1 (doubling); each increment held 24 hours; ASTM D2435/AASHTO T216; (2) constant rate of strain (CRS) — continuous loading at constant axial strain rate; ASTM D4186; requires base pore pressure measurement. Both define σ'p, Cc, and Cr from e-log σ'v. Sampling disturbance: problematic in soft sensitive clays; fixed piston or Laval samplers preferred; block samples best. Schmertmann (1955) method corrects laboratory curve for disturbance.
sections.body:
Incremental load (IL) consolidation test (ASTM D2435, AASHTO T216): Applies a series of vertical loads to a laterally confined specimen (typically 50-76 mm diameter, 20-25 mm height). Standard load schedule: LIR = 1 (doubling each increment). Each increment held for 24 hours (longer if secondary compression is significant). Measurements of vertical deformation vs. time for each load increment. Output: e-log σ'v or εv-log σ'v plot; preconsolidation stress σ'p; Cc (slope of normal consolidation line); Cr (recompression slope).

Constant rate of strain (CRS) consolidation test (ASTM D4186): Applies continuous loading at constant axial strain rate (0.05% to 1% per hour typical). Requires pore pressure measurement at base. Strain rate selected to maintain ratio of excess pore pressure to total stress of ≤ 5–10%. Faster than IL tests; continuous data gives better-defined σ'p. Useful for soft to medium clays.

Sampling disturbance effects: Stress relief from excavation/extraction, mechanical disturbance, and gas exsolution can all degrade sample quality. Table 6-1 characterizes sample quality from consolidation test results. Block samples and fixed-piston samples produce least disturbance; Shelby tube samples may show significant disturbance for soft sensitive clays (Figure 6-4). Schmertmann (1955) method (Figure 6-18) corrects laboratory curve for disturbance effects to produce 'field consolidation curve'.
key_points: IL test (ASTM D2435): LIR = 1 (doubling); each increment held 24 hrs; measures e-log σ'v
CRS test (ASTM D4186): continuous loading at constant strain rate; requires base pore pressure measurement
Sampling disturbance overestimates σ'p and distorts Cc; block samples and fixed-piston samplers preferred
Schmertmann (1955) method corrects for disturbance to obtain field compression curve

sections.title: Preconsolidation Stress, Compression Parameters, and Rate of Consolidation
sections.summary: Preconsolidation stress σ'p from IL tests by: Casagrande method (tangent + bisector construction), strain energy method (more consistent per Grozic et al. 2003), or tangent modulus method. OCR = σ'p/σ'vo. Compression index Cc from slope of normal consolidation line (log-space); recompression index Cr = 0.1–0.25 Cc typically. cv from Casagrande log-time (T90 = 0.848) or Taylor square root of time method. In situ: σ'p from CPT (qt), CPTU (u2), DMT (KD), FVT (su-FV), PMT (pL), SPT (N60) — all with significant scatter. ch from CPTU dissipation tests (Terzaghi monotonic or Tflex method). Cα/Cc typically 0.04 for most inorganic clays.
sections.body:
Preconsolidation stress σ'p from laboratory tests: (1) Casagrande method — graphical construction on e-log σ'v plot: tangent at point of maximum curvature, horizontal line, bisector, tangent to linear portion; σ'p at intersection. (2) Strain energy method (Becker et al. 1987) — σ'p at peak of strain energy vs. log σ'v plot; more objective and consistent (Figure 6-15). (3) Tangent modulus method — from CRS tests; σ'p at minimum of tangent modulus M.

OCR = σ'p / σ'vo. Table of OCR interpretation from IL tests. Correlations for σ'p or OCR from in-situ tests (Table 6-5/6-6): qt (CPT), u2 (CPTU), KD (DMT), su-FV (FVT), pL (PMT), N60 (SPT). Scatter in correlations is substantial — use multiple methods when possible.

Compression parameters: Cc = slope of normal consolidation line in e-log σ'v space. Cr = recompression slope (typically 0.1 to 0.25 Cc). Correlations of Cc with initial void ratio eo and LL (Table 6-12). Cr often from slope of unload-reload curve or from separate tests.

Coefficient of consolidation cv: Casagrande log-time method: cv = T90 × d²/t90 where T90 = 0.848 (Eq 6 from ASTM D2435). d = drainage path length = H/2 for double drainage. Taylor square root of time method: t90 from modified intercept.

ch from CPTU dissipation tests: ch from time for u to dissipate to baseline (Robertson et al. 1992 chart; modified time factor T* method). Horizontal consolidation governs for wick drains and stone columns.

Secondary compression: Cα = Cαε / (1+eo). Cα/Cc typically 0.04 for inorganic clays (Mesri and Godlewski 1977); higher for organic soils. Values for specific soils in Table 6-17.
key_points: Casagrande and strain energy methods for σ'p; strain energy more objective and consistent
Cc = slope of NC line (log-space); Cr ≈ 0.1–0.25 Cc; Cc correlates with eo and LL (Table 6-12)
cv (Casagrande): T90 × d²/t90; T90 = 0.848; d = H/2 for double drainage
ch from CPTU dissipation tests; Robertson et al. (1992) T*-based chart
Cα/Cc ≈ 0.04 for inorganic clays; higher for organic soils
